My name is Ash. Nice to meet you.

Numbers. You'll use these every single day, so we'll take them in two halves. One.
Two. The tone rises — like a question.
One, two, three, four, five. Listen.
Now you. Count to five with her — say each one before she does. One.
The money is baht. It's a short, plain word.
Five baht. Number first, then baht.
Five baht, with the polite ending — that's how she'd tell you a price.
Now the question you'll ask most. How much? Listen.

Say the first part — it's two syllables. Tao, rai. The second one rises.
How much? With the question ending.

At a stall you'll point at things. This one. Listen.
The second part means this. Say it.
The first part is a little word that means thing, or item — it goes in front. Say this one.
How much is this one? This one — how much — question ending.

The second half. Six. Short — it drops.
Seven. Short, and it drops too.
Eight. Also short and dropping. Six, seven, eight all sound like little taps.
Nine. This one drops, and it's longer.
Now all ten, on your own. She'll follow.

Now she'll tell you prices. After each one, say the number in English.
เก้าบาทค่ะ
You know the word for could I have — from could I have some water. Here it is with a number. Two of them, please. Listen.
ขอสองอันค่ะ
Could I have — two — and that little word for thing again, an. Two things. Say it.

Ask for one. Careful — for one, Thai people usually put the number after: thing, one.

One more word for shopping. To take — as in I'll take it, I'll have it. Listen.

And with not in front — I don't want it, I won't take it. Not, take. It's the polite way to say no thanks.
Put things together. Ask how much this one is.
